title: Confident Leaders Must Learn to Hedge
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article is aimed at leaders whose blunt, highly confident communication style makes them effective but hard to work with. Rather than urging them to be less direct, the author introduces hedging, prefacing an assertion with phrases like I think or it seems to me, as a way to soften delivery without diluting the underlying honesty. The piece offers a list of easy hedge phrases and explains that hedges invite dialogue rather than asserting unchallengeable certainty. It closes with a caveat: hedging can backfire for leaders who already come across as tentative, so the technique is specifically for those who tend to bulldoze.
points: Highly confident, blunt leaders are often valued for insight but penalized for how they make people feel
Hedging, prefacing a statement with phrases like I think or it seems to me, softens delivery without diluting honesty
A hedge invites interpretation and dialogue rather than asserting unchallengeable certainty
The caveat: leaders who already seem tentative can damage their credibility by overusing hedges
quotes: Delivering honesty without emotional regulation is a recipe for intimidation and perceptions of insensitivity.
The answer to this dilemma is that they don’t have to be less direct or honest. They simply need to learn how to add a hedge.
Hedging shifts advocacy from an absolute claim to a subjective impression open to interpretation.
Hedges invite interpretation and dialogue rather than asserting an indisputable certainty.
Leaders who speak more indirectly and with lower confidence can harm their credibility by using hedges, and so can confident leaders who use too many of them, too often.
